name: Gabriel Demombynes
headline: Economist. Manager of the Human Capital Project at the World Bank.
tagline: Scholar of AI and human capital
profile: Development economist and engineer leading the Human Capital Project. Twenty years across Africa, East Asia, and Latin America, combining operational delivery, policy dialogue, and rigorous evaluation to translate innovation into measurable outcomes in education, health, social protection, and jobs.
bio: Gabriel has been based in Bogotá, Manila, Hanoi, and Nairobi, and led the World Bank's Systematic Country Diagnostics for Colombia, the Philippines, and Vietnam as well as the Philippines COVID-19 Emergency Response Health Project. His analytical work spans nutrition in the Philippines, child survival in Kenya, learning poverty in Colombia, global COVID-19 mortality patterns, Vietnam's household registration system, the Millennium Villages Project, crime and violence in Central America and the Caribbean, and mobile-phone surveys in South Sudan.

He is best known for arguing for the greater use of the scientific method in evaluating international development programs. His work has appeared in academic journals and has been cited in the Financial Times, the Washington Post, and The Economist. He has taught economic development at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies and was Economic Policy Advisor to Howard Dean during the 2003–04 U.S. presidential campaign.

places.label: Colombia
places.blurb: Three years in Bogotá leading the World Bank's human development team for Colombia and Venezuela through the pandemic: a national seroprevalence program, a data dashboard for safe reopening, the vaccine production agenda, the 2022 Systematic Country Diagnostic update, and a new measure of learning poverty at the level of every municipality.

places.label: Philippines
places.role: Program Leader for Human Development, Brunei, Malaysia, Philippines, and Thailand
places.blurb: Four years in Manila. The work centered on why nearly one Filipino child in three is stunted, on the national ID system, on the 2019 Systematic Country Diagnostic, and, in 2020, on designing and leading the $100 million COVID-19 Emergency Response Health Project that grew into the country's $900 million pandemic and vaccination program.

highlight.title: The Philippines COVID-19 Emergency Response Project
text: When the pandemic reached the Philippines in March 2020, Gabriel led the World Bank team that designed and launched the country's emergency health response. As Task Team Leader, with Sutayut Osornprasop, he took a $100 million loan from concept to Board approval on 23 April 2020, in a matter of weeks, under the Bank's global COVID-19 fast-track program, with the Department of Health as implementing agency.

The project's objective was to strengthen the country's capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to COVID-19 and to build lasting public health preparedness: intensive-care and laboratory equipment for hospitals, personal protective equipment, isolation and quarantine facilities, and upgraded national and regional reference laboratories. Additional financing of $500 million in March 2021 and $300 million in December 2021 turned it into the backbone of the national vaccination campaign.

mvp.intro: In 2010, Gabriel and Michael Clemens of the Center for Global Development asked a simple question about the Millennium Villages Project, the high-profile package intervention led by Jeffrey Sachs: how would anyone know whether it worked? Comparing trends at the project sites in Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria with trends in the surrounding regions, they found that the project's before-and-after comparisons attributed to the intervention improvements that were happening everywhere. The exchange that followed, in blogs, seminars, The Guardian, and The Lancet, became a case study in transparency and the scientific method in development.

timeline.text: "When Does Rigorous Impact Evaluation Make a Difference?" released as CGD Working Paper 225 and World Bank WPS 5477; first Africa Can post, "Evaluating the Millennium Villages."
Reply to the MVP's response and a seminar with comments from Jeff Sachs.
Shanta Devarajan, World Bank Africa chief economist, calls the paper "the first evaluation of the MVP."
"Millennium Villages Project continues to systematically overstate its effects."
"Millennium Villages Project needs proper evaluation," The Guardian, Poverty Matters. Sachs replies in the same forum.
Peer-reviewed version published in the Journal of Development Effectiveness.

Letter in The Lancet with Jesse Bump and Lawrence Haddad; the MVP corrects its Lancet paper and its lead author departs. A companion post shows under-five mortality fell more slowly at MVP sites than nationally.
Independent critique of the MVP's stunting claims in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.
"The New Transparency in Development Economics: Lessons from the Millennium Villages Controversy," CGD Working Paper 342 and World Economics.
The MVP's own retrospective endline evaluation appears in The Lancet Global Health, and a 2021 paper by Mitchell, Gelman, and Sachs sets out to reconcile the competing evaluations.
